question: Regarding the vascular anatomy relevant to epistaxis: which of the following correctly identifies Little's area and Woodruff's plexus?

answers.text: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) is on the posterior lateral nasal wall under the inferior turbinate; Woodruff's plexus is on the anteroinferior nasal septum.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — the sites are transposed. Little's area is on the ANTEROINFERIOR nasal septum (Kiesselbach's plexus), and Woodruff's plexus is on the POSTERIOR LATERAL nasal wall (under the posterior end of the inferior turbinate). This is a classic examination trap.

answers.text: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) is on the anteroinferior nasal septum and is the source of 90% of anterior epistaxis; Woodruff's plexus is on the posterior lateral nasal wall under the posterior end of the inferior turbinate and is the source of most posterior epistaxis.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Little's area is the confluence of five arteries (anterior and posterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and superior labial) on the anteroinferior septum — visible and accessible on anterior rhinoscopy. Woodruff's plexus (sphenopalatine and posterior pharyngeal arteries) lies deep on the posterior lateral wall and is the usual source of severe posterior epistaxis in elderly hypertensive patients.

answers.text: Both Little's area and Woodruff's plexus are located on the nasal septum, differing only in their anterior-posterior position.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Woodruff's plexus is on the LATERAL nasal wall (under the posterior inferior turbinate), not on the septum. Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) is on the septum. This anatomical distinction explains why posterior epistaxis cannot be controlled by simple anterior nasal packing.

answers.text: Little's area is supplied solely by the anterior ethmoidal artery and is the source of posterior epistaxis in elderly hypertensives.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect on both counts. Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) receives contributions from five arterial sources, not just the anterior ethmoidal. It is the source of ANTERIOR (not posterior) epistaxis. Posterior epistaxis in elderly hypertensives arises from Woodruff's plexus.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is a high-yield anatomy point. Remember: Little's area is anterior and septal; Woodruff's plexus is posterior and lateral. Never transpose them.
Correct. Little's area = anteroinferior septum = anterior epistaxis (90%). Woodruff's plexus = posterior lateral wall = posterior epistaxis (10%, more severe).
